title: History and Appreciation of Art (7th AD to 12th AD)
summary: The post-Gupta period is known for progress in temple architecture and sculpture. The dynasties were the Pallavas, Cholas and Hoysalas in the south and the Palas, Senas and Gangas in the east. At Mahabalipuram (Mamallapuram) are the Pancharathas and Mandapas. The Pallavas and the Western Chalukyas are remembered for sculpture; the Cholas and Hoysalas for temple projects. Chola artists excelled in bronze casting with delicate, rhythmic body movements; important Chola temples are Gangaikondacholapuram and Brihadeswara. Hoysala art mixed intricate design and detailed study, with temple sculptures as part of the architecture. In the east, the Ganga rulers built the Mukteswar, Lingaraja and Rajarani temples in Orissa. The centres of art shifted to southern and eastern India.

Medium: stone. Period: Pallava, 7th century AD. Place: Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram, near Chennai). Size: about 91 ft x 152 ft. Artist: unknown. It is a relief on two huge boulders with a cleft in between and a crowd of life-size human and animal figures – gods, demigods and sages in flying position – all facing the cleft; there is much movement in the upper part, while the lower part calms down and the ascetics sit in meditation. According to some scholars it is Gangavatarana, with Shiva receiving the Ganga in his hair (the larger four-armed figure with a trident to the right of the cleft); others call it Arjuna's Penance because a male figure at one end is in meditation. It has enormous speed and monumentality, soft round figures and close observation of animals (sleeping baby elephant, monkeys, a deer scratching its nose).

Medium: stone (soft schist). Period: Hoysala. Place: Belur. Size: about 3 ft. Artist: unknown. The Hoysala dynasty rose around the middle of the 11th century and ended in the mid 14th century; its capital Dvarasamudra is modern Halebid; the earliest major temples are at Belur; other major Hoysala temples are the Hoysaleswara temple at Halebid and the Kesava temple at Somnathpur. Hoysala sculptures show deep carving and undercutting, soft rhythms of the body contours and delicate, intricate designs, made possible by the soft stone, which gives a rich surface texture. In the sculpture the incident is shown in layers with Krishna as the central heroic figure, and human beings and cattle in different layers; the animals are lively; the figures have heavy breasts and buttocks, elaborate jewellery and typical Indian hairstyle.

Medium: stone. Period: Ganga dynasty, 12th century AD. Place: Konarka, Orissa. Size: a little more than life size. The Sun Temple at Konarka, near Puri on the eastern coast, was built by King Narasimhadeva I of the Ganga dynasty in the form of a chariot drawn by horses. It is famous for its gigantic structure and larger-than-life sculptures, usually in black stone, which have some affinity with the later Bengal style of the Pala period. The modelling is tight, the face broad and smiling, the works robust with loose plasticity. The female musicians on the terraces above the bottom and middle tiers are boldly carved with movement and volume, each with a different instrument; the Surasundari is shown with a drum; the slight tilt of the head, the rhythmic limbs, soft carving of ornaments and folds of drapery add to the rhythm.

case.passage: The Post Gupta period in India is known for the progress in temple architecture and sculpture. Major dynasties like Pallavas, Cholas, Hoysalas in the south and Palas, Senas and Gangas in the east patronized this progress. In the south, at Mahabalipuram or Mamallapuram, we see the Pancharathas and the Mandapa structures. While Pallavas and their rivals, Western Chalukyans are remembered for their sculptural activities, Cholas and Hoysalas would be always remembered for their temple projects. Chola artists excelled in the techniques of bronze casting. The Chola period has also given us temples like the Gangaikondacholapuram temple and the Brihadeswara temple.

vsa: Hoysala period is remembered for the stone sculptures. Why?

Hoysala sculptures show deep carving and undercutting made possible by the soft stone, which gives a rich surface texture and intricate details. They have soft rhythms of the body contours and delicate designs, and the sculptures form an intrinsic part of the temple architecture.

or: Give a general introduction to Hoysala art.

The Hoysala style is named after the Hoysala dynasty of the Deccan (mid 11th to mid 14th century); the capital was Dvarasamudra (Halebid) and the earliest major temples are at Belur. Temples were decorated with sculptures forming part of the architecture, with deep carving, undercutting, soft body rhythms and intricate designs.

vsa: Name the capital of the Pallava dynasty rulers. Mention two main features of the statues made during this dynasty.
The capital was Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram). Pallava sculptures are gentle, soft and rounded, with enormous speed and monumentality; the animal figures show close observation of nature.
Write a very short note on 'Krishna Supporting Mount Govardhana'.

It is a stone sculpture (about 3 ft) of the Hoysala period from Belur. Krishna stands as the central heroic figure with human beings and cattle shown in layers; the animals are lively and the figures have elaborate jewellery; deep carving shows the mastery of the artist.

It is a little more than life-size stone figure of a female musician from the 12th-century Sun temple in Orissa, shown with a drum. The big smiling face, slight tilt of the head, rhythmic limbs, soft carving of ornaments and folds of drapery give graceful beauty and rhythm.
Describe Arjuna's Penance in a few lines.

A Pallava relief (7th century AD) at Mamallapuram, about 91 ft x 152 ft, on two huge boulders with a cleft in between. Life-size gods, demigods, sages and animals face the cleft; some think it shows the descent of Ganga received by Shiva and others Arjuna's penance.
Name two famous Chola temples and the metal in which Chola artists were expert.
Chola artists were expert in bronze casting; famous Chola temples are the Gangaikondacholapuram temple and the Brihadeswara temple, noted for simplicity, monumentality and majestic quality.
Which temples were built by the Ganga rulers in Orissa?
The Mukteswar temple, the Lingaraja temple, the Rajarani temple and the Sun temple at Konarka.
sa: What are the characteristics of the 'Krishna Supporting Mount Govardhana' sculpture? Where is it located?

It is located at Belur and belongs to the Hoysala period (stone, about 3 ft). Krishna is the central heroic figure with human beings and cattle in different layers, a stance with rhythmic limbs that brings softness; the animals are lively; there are heavy breasts and buttocks, elaborate jewellery and typical Indian hairstyle; deep carving and undercutting in soft stone show the mastery of the artist.
What are the characteristics of the Konarka 'Surasundari' sculpture?

It is a little more than life size, in stone of the Ganga dynasty (12th century). The modelling is tight, the face broad with a smile, the work robust with loose plasticity. Female musicians on the terraces are boldly carved, full of movement and volume; the Surasundari is shown with a drum, with a slight tilt of the head, rhythmic limbs, soft ornament carving and rhythmic folds of drapery.

or: Where is the Sun Temple of Konark? What are the characteristics of the Konark sculptures?

The Sun Temple stands at Konarka near Puri in Orissa; it was built by Narasimhadeva I in the form of a chariot. The sculptures are gigantic, larger than life size and usually of black stone, with tight modelling, broad smiling faces and robust bodies.

sa: It is a Pallava relief (7th century AD) on two huge boulders at Mamallapuram, about 91 ft x 152 ft, with a cleft between them. Life-size gods, demigods, sages and animals face the cleft; the upper part is full of movement and the lower part calm with meditating ascetics. It may show Shiva receiving the Ganga or Arjuna's penance. It has speed, monumentality and soft, round figures; animals like the sleeping baby elephant show close observation.
Write the main characteristics of Hoysala sculptures.

They show deep carving and undercutting made possible by the soft schist stone, rich surface texture, soft rhythms of body contours and delicate intricate designs; sculptures are part of the temple architecture; examples are at Belur, Halebid and Somnathpur.
la: Explain Arjuna's Penance (Gangavatarana): its medium, period, place, size and artistic features.

Arjuna's Penance is a stone relief of the Pallava period (7th century AD) at Mamallapuram near Chennai, about 91 ft x 152 ft, by an unknown artist. It is carved on two huge boulders with a cleft between them; life-size gods, demigods, sages and animals face the cleft. The upper part has movement and energy; the lower part is calm with meditating ascetics. Some scholars read it as Gangavatarana (Shiva receiving the Ganga in his hair) and others as Arjuna's penance. The figures are soft and round, the animals (baby elephant, monkeys, deer scratching its nose) show close observation, and it is a masterpiece of southern Indian sculpture.
Write a note on Hoysala art with reference to the Krishna Govardhana sculpture.

The Hoysala style (mid 11th–mid 14th century) developed in the Deccan with capital Dvarasamudra (Halebid); major temples are at Belur, Halebid and Somnathpur. Temples were decorated with sculptures that form part of the architecture. The soft stone allowed deep carving and undercutting, soft rhythms and intricate details. The Krishna Supporting Mount Govardhana from Belur (about 3 ft) shows Krishna as the central heroic figure with humans and cattle in layers, lively animals, heavy breasts and buttocks, rich jewellery and typical hairstyle, showing the artist's mastery.
